title: Input Capture: Keylogging
summary: Keylogging records the keystrokes a user produces so that credentials can be recovered as they are typed, which is valuable when stored secrets are unavailable or strongly protected and may require long term interception before anything useful is captured. Implementations differ widely. User mode loggers hook the programming interface callbacks that deliver keystroke messages, or poll the asynchronous key state repeatedly. Kernel mode and driver based loggers sit closer to the hardware and read raw input before applications receive it, which also lets them capture keystrokes in windows they do not own. Other variants modify registry settings or filter device stacks, and some compromise the operating system of a network device to read console login sessions directly. Defenders rarely find keyloggers by file name. Stronger signals are a process reading keyboard input while owning no visible window, unexpected loading of input related libraries or drivers, new or altered keyboard filter registrations, unusual persistence entries, and files or network flows containing long streams of printable text.

beginner.definition: Keylogging means secretly recording what someone types on a keyboard. Every key press is saved, so the attacker can later read passwords, messages and card numbers. Some keyloggers are ordinary programs, and others are small pieces of software that sit close to the keyboard hardware. The person typing sees nothing unusual, because the keyboard behaves exactly as it always does.
beginner.whyItMatters: People type passwords all day long, and those passwords are valid the moment they are captured. A keylogger can also record anything else typed on that machine, including private messages and payment details. It hides well, because typing looks completely normal to anyone watching. A keylogger that runs for weeks may collect hundreds of credentials. That is why it is worth knowing where to look for the signs.
howItWorks: Every key press reaches the operating system as an event that programs can receive.
A program may ask to receive those events and quietly save them to a file.
Some loggers read the current keyboard state again and again, which is called polling.
Others install a small driver that sits between the keyboard and the operating system.
Kernel level loggers can capture keys even when a different window has focus.
The collected text is stored locally or sent out for the attacker to read later.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared flat where the front door has a keypad instead of a key. A small camera is hidden above the pad and records every button pressed. Residents still enter their own codes, and the door still opens normally, so nobody suspects anything. The camera never touches the lock and never needs a key of its own. It simply watches what people already do, and the recording hands the intruder every code in the whole building.
takeaways: Keyloggers can work in user programs or deeper, close to the keyboard hardware.
They do not need to break encryption, because they read input before it is protected.
Unusual keyboard access and long captured text are stronger clues than file names.

objectives: Explain how keystroke events travel through an operating system.
Describe the difference between user mode hooking and kernel level capture.
Identify artefacts that suggest unauthorised keyboard capture on a host.
Explain why keyloggers are difficult to find by file inspection alone.
Describe how to separate authorised accessibility tools from malicious loggers.
